Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Academy Award-winning composer Maurice Jarre, who scored movies including "Doctor Zhivago" and "Lawrence of Arabia" among others, died Sunday from cancer in Los Angeles. He was 84. Movie composer Maurice Jarre pictured at the Berlin International Film Festival last month. Jarre enjoyed an illustrious career, working with Hollywood directing legends including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock and, most notably, David Lean. Fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat, who interviewed Jarre for The Screening Room at the Berlin International Film Festival last month, told CNN Monday: "Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being."  Watch tribute to Maurice Jarre » . Jarre won Oscars in 1963 and 1966 for his collaborations on the Lean movies "Lawrence of Arabia" and "Doctor Zhivago" respectively. He then mustered a further six Oscar nominations but his third award came once again through a further collaboration with Lean on " A Passage to India" in 1984. He then swapped orchestral composition to become a pioneer of electronic scoring, working on the music for, among others, "Ghost," "Witness," "Dead Poet's Society" and "Fatal Attraction." At the same time his son Jean-Michel Jarre became one of the world's best known electronic musicians with global hits such as "Oxygene" and huge outdoor concerts. His final movie composition was for the 2000 film "I Dreamed of Africa." Jarre's career included symphonies, ballet and theatre but it was for his 150 film scores that he was presented with an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month - almost half a century after producer Sam Spiegel hired him to work on "Lawrence of Arabia." Festival director Dieter Kosslick said in a statement late last year: "Film composers often are in the shadows of great directors and acting stars. It's different with Maurice Jarre; the music of 'Doctor Zhivago,' like much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgotten in the history of cinema." Speaking in Berlin to double-Oscar nominee Desplat -- who himself scored "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" and "The Queen" -- Jarre said: "I never really had a 'bust-up' with a good director. A good director will always find an intellectual understanding. And that's what was great - I had an opportunity with all these people. I don't think I can say that I ever worked with a bad director." But Jarre also said that directing legends of the rank of Huston and Hitchock had disappeared and no longer existed, adding: "The only problem is now, there is more and more bad music that goes 'dang dang dang dang dang...' So...it's better to turn off the music, and listen to a concert of Mozart." Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to this report.

At the same time, his son Jean-Michel Jarre became one of the world’s best-known electronic musicians, achieving global success with works such as “Oxygene” and staging enormous outdoor concerts.

Maurice Jarre’s final film composition was for the 2000 movie “I Dreamed of Africa.”

Maurice Jarre, the Academy Award-winning French composer whose sweeping music for *Lawrence of Arabia* and *Doctor Zhivago* became inseparable from the films themselves, died of cancer in Los Angeles at the age of 84. His death prompted filmmakers, musicians, and admirers to look back on a career that spanned more than five decades and helped define the sound of modern cinema.

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre initially studied engineering before turning to music. He trained in composition, percussion, and conducting at the Paris Conservatory, then began his professional career in the theater. After serving as musical director of the Théâtre National Populaire, he moved increasingly into film, where his talent for combining memorable themes with unusual instrumentation soon attracted international attention.

Jarre’s most celebrated partnership was with British director David Lean. Their first collaboration, the 1962 epic *Lawrence of Arabia*, produced one of the most recognizable orchestral scores in film history and earned Jarre his first Academy Award. He won again for Lean’s *Doctor Zhivago* in 1965, whose romantic “Lara’s Theme” became a worldwide popular success, and for *A Passage to India* in 1984. He also composed the music for Lean’s *Ryan’s Daughter*.

Although best known for grand orchestral writing, Jarre was not confined to a single style. He frequently experimented with percussion, non-Western instruments, synthesizers, and electronic textures. His score for Peter Weir’s *Witness*, for example, relied heavily on synthesizers and demonstrated his ability to create atmosphere and emotional intensity without the large orchestra associated with his earlier work. His willingness to combine traditional and electronic sounds helped broaden the expressive possibilities of film music.

Over the course of his career, Jarre wrote music for roughly 150 films. His credits included *The Longest Day*, *The Train*, *The Man Who Would Be King*, *The Year of Living Dangerously*, *Fatal Attraction*, *Gorillas in the Mist*, *Dead Poets Society*, and *Ghost*. He worked with prominent directors across Europe and Hollywood, adapting his approach to historical epics, intimate dramas, thrillers, and romances.

In addition to his three Oscars, Jarre received numerous nominations and international honors. Shortly before his death, he was recognized at the Berlin International Film Festival for his lifetime contribution to cinema. Tributes from fellow artists emphasized both the emotional power of his melodies and his skill at serving a film’s story without overwhelming it.

Jarre was also part of a prominent musical family. His son, Jean-Michel Jarre, became an internationally known composer and pioneer of electronic music, while another son, Kevin Jarre, worked as a screenwriter.

With his gift for expansive themes, distinctive rhythms, and inventive orchestration, Maurice Jarre created music that often outlived the films for which it was written. His three Academy Awards, pioneering use of electronic sound, and vast body of work established him as one of the most influential and internationally recognized composers in cinema history.
